messages.author: e797750083d5125f
messages.subject: microbial dynamics
parts:
I've used polar stacked barplots to visualize the difference in
bacterial community composition over a seasonal study and it looks
great.

Now I want to combine this data with normal environmental factors such
as temperature, plotted as a gradient at the outer edge of my polar
barplots. Building gradient circles on other gradient circles, not
unlike genome atlases. I would like to base this gradient on the
temperature data that I have, the gradient going from low temperature
indicated by let's say blue to high temperature with red color, and
then have a legend for the temperature, low, medium, high or 5, 10,
15, 20°C.

Is there a way to incorporate all information in one graph?

I would greatly appreciate any help you can provide.

messages.author: 85435c7e2689700c
messages.subject: Re: microbial dynamics
parts:
It should be possible as long as you don't need more than one color
scale. My take would be to use geom_tile and specify a y-value higher
than the maximum in your inner graph. If you make your data available
I could look at it as I'm also working with circular heat maps as part
of my project...

best wishes

Thomas

messages.author: 85435c7e2689700c
messages.subject: Re: microbial dynamics
parts:
As I said in the initial reply, the architecture right now does not
support multiple fill scales. This means that it is not easy to have
multiple rings in one plot. I have overcome this by building the heat
maps manually using a lot of for loops, but this can get quite
heavy...

The second problem is that I did not realize that the fill scale was
already used for building the stacked bar/pie chart, so even one outer
ring would require some data joggling...

to create your outer rings it will be necessary to manually calculate
the associated color for each tile and build the ring iteratively in a
for loop like:

for (i in 1:nrow(data.a)){
p <- p + geom_tile(data=data.a[i, 'Salinity'], aes(x=Date, y=y.pos),
fill=colour, width=1, height=tile.height)
}

where y.pos is a value higher than the height of your barplot,
tile.height is the width of the ring and color is your calculated
color for the single tile.

The problem with this approach is that you do not get legends
associated with the rings, but it is the best I can think of...

good luck

Thomas
